stages.title: Forks
stages.hook: One move, two targets, and your opponent can only save one. How can you set that up on purpose rather than by luck?
explain: A fork is a move in which one piece attacks two or more enemy pieces at once. Because the opponent has only one move, they usually cannot save everything. The attacker wins material. Any piece can fork, but knights are special: their L-shaped attack cannot be blocked, and they are often not attacked by the pieces they fork.

The most powerful fork is a check combined with an attack on another piece, because the opponent must answer the check first. A knight that checks the king and attacks a queen is a "royal fork". Queens fork too, and even pawns: a pawn that advances to attack two pieces is hard to answer.

To find forks, look for squares that attack two targets and are safe from capture. Ask: can an enemy piece capture my forking piece? And are the targets protected? A fork on protected pieces still wins material if the forker is worth less than the targets.

example.q: White knight on e4, Black king g8, Black queen d7, White king g1 and a white pawn on a2. White to move. What wins the queen?
steps: Look for a knight move that checks the king and attacks the queen.
Nf6+ attacks g8 (check) and d7 (queen) at once.
The king moves out of check and the knight captures the queen: Nxd7.

stages.title: Pins and skewers
stages.hook: A piece stands still, not because it is blocked, but because moving would be a disaster. How can an attacker freeze a piece without touching it?
explain: A pin happens when an attacking bishop, rook or queen attacks a piece that has another more valuable piece (or the king) behind it on the same line. If the pinned piece moves, the piece behind it is exposed. An absolute pin is a pin against the king: the pinned piece cannot legally move off the line. A relative pin is against a lesser piece: the move is legal but costs material.

A skewer is the reverse. The more valuable piece is in front and is attacked. When it moves away, the piece behind it is captured. For example, a rook gives check to a king, and a queen stands behind the king on the same line.
To exploit a pin, attack the pinned piece again, with a pawn if possible. To break a pin, move the piece behind, block, or capture the pinner.

example.q: Black king d4, Black queen g4, White pawn b3, White rook a1, White king h1. White to move. What wins the queen?
steps: The king and queen are on the same rank: d4 then g4.
Ra4+ attacks the king; the queen stands behind it on the same line.
The king must leave, and then Rxg4 takes the queen.

stages.title: Discovered attacks
stages.hook: A magician moves the curtain and reveals something behind it. Can a chess piece move out of the way and reveal an attack?
explain: A discovered attack happens when you move a piece and uncover an attack by another piece behind it. Two things now happen at once: the moved piece does one job, and the uncovered piece does another. The opponent cannot deal with both.

A discovered check is the strongest kind. The moved piece uncovers a check on the king, so the opponent must answer the check, and the moved piece can then capture something or make a threat for free. When the moving piece itself also gives check, this is called a double check, and the king must move.

To find discovered attacks, look for a long-range piece (bishop, rook, queen) with one of your own pieces in front. Ask: where can the front piece go with gain? Take a piece, attack a queen, or create a fork.

example.q: White rook e1, White knight e5, White king g1. Black king e8, Black queen d8. White to move. What wins the queen?
steps: The knight on e5 blocks the rook on the e-file to the black king.
Any knight move uncovers check, so choose one that attacks the queen safely.
Nc6+ is a discovered check and also attacks the queen on d8. Then Nxd8.

stages.title: Double attacks
stages.hook: You attack your opponent's queen and, with the same move, threaten checkmate. Can they stop both?
explain: A double attack is a single move that creates two threats at once. The threats can be against two pieces, or against a piece and a checkmate, or against a piece and a pawn promotion. A fork is a double attack made by one piece; a double attack can also come from two pieces, for example when a discovered attack uncovers a second threat.

Why does it work? The opponent has one move. If both threats are real, and no single reply meets them both, you win something. A reply that handles both is possible only if there is a move that, for example, captures the attacker, checks you, or defends both targets at once.
Before you play a double attack, find the best defence for your opponent. Look at forcing replies: checks, captures and counter-threats. A double attack that allows a counter-check can fail.

example.q: Your queen attacks an undefended rook and also threatens mate in one. Your opponent can stop only one. What do you win?
steps: List the two threats: capture the rook, and mate.
Stopping the mate leaves the rook, so a rook can fall.
If you stop the rook, you give mate. So the opponent must stop the mate and lose the rook.

stages.title: Tactical combinations
stages.hook: A player gives up their queen on purpose and ends up winning. How can a sacrifice be the best move?
explain: A combination is a forcing series of moves, usually with a sacrifice, that leads to a gain. The moves are forcing: checks, captures and threats that the opponent must answer. Because the replies are forced, you can calculate the whole line to the end.

Common themes inside combinations are deflection (forcing a defender away), decoy (luring a piece onto a bad square), removing the defender, and back-rank mate. A sacrifice gives up material for a bigger gain, such as checkmate or more material back.
To find a combination, look for weaknesses: an exposed king, an undefended piece or a piece that guards something. Then ask: what forcing move can I make, and what must the opponent reply?

example.q: White queen d3, rook d1, king g1. Black queen d8, rook e8, king g8, pawns f7 g7 h7. White to move. What wins?
steps: Find a forcing capture: Qxd8 takes the queen, and attacks the rook on e8.
If Black recaptures Rxd8, then Rxd8 is checkmate along the 8th rank (pawns block the king).
If Black does not recapture, White is a queen ahead.

stages.title: Pawn structures
stages.hook: Pawns can never go backwards, so each pawn move is a promise for the rest of the game. How do the pawns shape the whole plan?
explain: Pawn structure is the arrangement of pawns. It is important because pawns cannot move backwards, so changes are permanent. Good structure supports your pieces and leaves your opponent targets.

Some common features: a doubled pawn means two pawns of the same colour on one file; an isolated pawn has no friendly pawns on the neighbouring files; a backward pawn is behind its neighbours and cannot safely advance; a passed pawn has no enemy pawns ahead of it on its file or on neighbouring files, so it can run to promotion. A pawn chain is a diagonal line of pawns protecting each other. Pawn islands are groups of pawns separated by files with no friendly pawns.

Weak pawns create weak squares in front of them. Strong structures, such as a pawn chain or a protected passed pawn, are advantages. Good players try to give their opponent weak pawns and keep their own healthy.

example.q: White pawns on a2, c2, c3, f2, g2, h2. Find the doubled pawns and count the pawn islands.
steps: Two pawns on the c file, c2 and c3, are doubled.
The a pawn stands alone (no pawn on the b file), the c pawns are alone (no b or d pawns), and f, g and h are together.
That gives three groups: a, c and f-g-h.

stages.title: Positional evaluation
stages.hook: Two positions have the same pieces, but one side is clearly better. What do strong players see that a piece count does not show?
explain: To evaluate a position, count material first: pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9. Then look at other factors: king safety, piece activity (how many squares pieces control), pawn structure, control of the centre and open files, and space. Having the two bishops against a bishop and a knight (the bishop pair) is often a small plus, especially in open positions.

Material is not everything. A rook is worth about five pawns, but a rook locked behind its own pawns may be less useful than an active knight. A passed pawn or an attack on the king can be worth more than material. On the other hand, a material lead usually wins if you stay safe and trade pieces.

A good method: compare both kings, then the pieces, then the pawns. Ask: Whose king is safer? Whose pieces are more active? Who has the better pawn structure? Then choose a plan that improves your worst piece.

example.q: White: queen, 2 rooks, bishop, knight, 5 pawns. Black: queen, 2 rooks, 2 bishops, 4 pawns. Who leads in material?
steps: White leads by 1 point, but Black has the bishop pair.

misc.right: Material usually matters most, but king safety, activity and structure can outweigh a small lead.

stages.title: Basic endgames
stages.hook: When most pieces are gone, a lone king can suddenly be a fighter. How do you win a game with just a king and one or two pieces?
explain: The endgame is the stage with few pieces. The king becomes a strong piece, so bring it to the centre. Key winning ideas: promote a pawn, and checkmate with a queen or rook. A king and queen can force checkmate against a lone king; a king and rook can too. A lone king against king and pawn depends on opposition: kings face each other with one square between them, and the player who does not have to move has the opposition and can force the other king aside.

Not every extra piece wins. King and bishop, or king and knight, against a lone king is a draw because mate is not possible. Two knights cannot force checkmate against a lone king. Beware of stalemate: when you are far ahead, make sure the enemy king has a legal move or is in check.
In pawn endings, a passed pawn far from the enemy king is strong. A rook pawn (a or h file) is a special case: the defending king can sometimes reach the corner in front of the pawn and draw.

example.q: White king f6, queen g2. Black king h8. White to move. Find mate in one.
steps: Black king on h8 has two squares to go: g8 and h7.
Qg7 attacks both squares and is protected by the king on f6.
The black king cannot capture the queen, so Qg7 is checkmate.

stages.title: Multi-step reasoning and calculation
stages.hook: To choose a good move you often need to look several moves ahead. How can you keep it all in your head without getting lost?
explain: Calculation means looking at sequences of moves in your head. A good method is to list candidate moves, then check forcing moves first: checks, captures and threats. For each, picture the position after your move, then the best reply, then your next move. Count material at the end of the line.

When counting a sequence of captures, add what you win and subtract what you lose, from your side. For example: your knight (3) takes a pawn (1), a pawn takes your knight, and your queen takes that pawn. You gained 1 + 1 = 2 and lost 3, so the net is −1. Recount at the end.

Multi-step reasoning also applies to distances and races. A king moves one square in any direction, so it needs as many moves as the larger of the file or rank difference. Pawns in a race: count the moves each needs to promote, and remember who moves first.

example.q: A white knight takes a pawn. A black pawn takes the knight. A white queen takes that pawn. What is the net material change for White? (pawn = 1, knight = 3)
steps: White gains a pawn: +1.
White loses the knight: −3, so the running total is −2.
White gains the pawn on the recapture: +1, so the total is −1.
